overview:
Ecuador takes its name from the equator, the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth that passes just north of its capital, Quito. It sits on the northwest coast of South America between Colombia and Peru, and although it is one of the continent's smaller countries, about 277,000 km² or roughly the size of Colorado, it packs in four very different worlds: the Pacific coast, the Andes mountains, the Amazon rainforest and the Galápagos Islands, about 1,000 kilometers out to sea.

About 18 million people live in Ecuador. Quito, at about 2,850 meters, is the second-highest capital city in the world and has one of the best-preserved colonial old towns in the Americas. Guayaquil, on the coast, is the biggest city and main port.

Spanish is the main language, and Kichwa, the language of the Inca, is spoken by many Indigenous people in the highlands. Ecuador is a republic with an elected president, and it has used the US dollar as its money since 2000. Bananas, shrimp, oil, roses and cacao are its main exports.
landAndNature:
Two chains of the Andes run through Ecuador, forming an "Avenue of the Volcanoes." Cotopaxi, a snow-capped cone of about 5,900 meters, is one of the highest active volcanoes on Earth, and Chimborazo, about 6,260 meters, is the point on the planet farthest from the Earth's center because the globe bulges at the equator. East of the mountains, the Amazon lowlands steam with rain, home to jaguars, pink dolphins, anacondas and more kinds of birds than all of North America.

The Galápagos Islands, born from volcanoes, are famous for animals found nowhere else: giant tortoises that live more than 100 years, marine iguanas that swim in the sea, blue-footed boobies, and the only penguins that live north of the equator. Charles Darwin's visit in 1835 helped him develop the theory of evolution.
peopleAndCulture:
Most Ecuadorians are mestizo, of mixed Indigenous and Spanish heritage, and around a fifth are Indigenous, especially Kichwa-speaking peoples of the Andes and Shuar and Waorani communities of the Amazon. Highland markets like Otavalo overflow with woven ponchos, and women there wear embroidered blouses and layers of gold beads.

Food changes with altitude: ceviche of shrimp and encebollado fish soup on the coast; potato patties called llapingachos, roasted corn and hearty soups in the mountains. Soccer is the top sport, and ecuavoley, a three-a-side volleyball played with a heavy ball, is a homegrown favorite. The Inti Raymi sun festival in June and the New Year's Eve burning of "año viejo" effigies are lively traditions. The fine straw hats sold as Panama hats are woven in the Ecuadorian town of Montecristi.
history:
The Valdivia culture on Ecuador's coast made some of the oldest pottery in the Americas about 5,500 years ago. Highland kingdoms later fell to the Inca in the late 1400s, and the Inca emperor Atahualpa was born in the north. Spanish soldiers arrived in 1534 and founded Quito on the ruins of an Inca city.

Quito's citizens made one of the first calls for independence in Spanish America on August 10, 1809, and freedom was won at the Battle of Pichincha in 1822. Ecuador belonged to Gran Colombia until 1830, then became its own republic. The 1900s brought cocoa and banana booms, oil discoveries in the Amazon, border wars with Peru that ended with a 1998 treaty, and frequent changes of government. A 2008 constitution made Ecuador the first country to give legal rights to nature itself.
funFacts: Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo is the farthest point from the planet's center, farther than Everest.
Ecuador exports more bananas than any other country in the world.
Panama hats are not from Panama; they have been woven in Ecuador for centuries.
Quito and Kraków were the first two cities ever named UNESCO World Heritage Sites, in 1978.
Galápagos giant tortoises can weigh over 250 kilograms and live well past 100 years.
Ecuador has no currency of its own; it has used US dollars since 2000.
